question: A 59-year-old man presents to the emergency department with right-sided weakness and an inability to speak for the past 2 hours. His wife says he was gardening in his backyard when he suddenly lost balance and fell down. The patient has a past medical history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and coronary artery disease. Two years ago, he was admitted to the coronary intensive care unit with an anterolateral myocardial infarction. He has not been compliant with his medications since he was discharged. On physical examination, his blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, pulse is 110/min and irregular, temperature is 36.6°C (97.8°F), and respiratory rate is 18/min. Strength is 2/5 in both his right upper and right lower extremities. His right calf is edematous with visible varicose veins. Which of the following is the best method to detect the source of this patient’s stroke?

options.opa: Duplex ultrasound of his right leg

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Right-sided weakness and inability to speak" -> "suggestive of a stroke" -> "consider imaging studies to detect the source" -> 90% CHAIN: "Hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and coronary artery disease" -> "increased risk for stroke" -> "prompt evaluation needed" -> 85% CHAIN: "Past anterolateral myocardial infarction" -> "increased risk for embolic stroke" -> "consider cardiac evaluation" -> 80% CHAIN: "Non-compliance with medications" -> "increased risk for stroke recurrence" -> "emphasize medication adherence" -> 75% CHAIN: "Right calf edema and varicose veins" -> "suggestive of venous thromboembolism" -> "consider lower extremity ultrasound" -> 90%
enhanced_information: The best method to detect the source of this patient's stroke is carotid duplex ultrasound. The patient's presentation of right-sided weakness and inability to speak, along with his medical history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and coronary artery disease, increases his risk for stroke. Given the possibility of embolic stroke due to his past myocardial infarction and non-compliance with medications, a carotid duplex can help identify any carotid artery disease contributing to the stroke. The presence of right calf edema and varicose veins suggests a venous thromboembolism, which can be evaluated separately with a lower extremity ultrasound.

Given the possibility of embolic stroke due to his past myocardial infarction and non-compliance with medications, carotid duplex ultrasound is the best method to detect any carotid artery disease contributing to the stroke. The presence of right calf edema and varicose veins suggests a venous thromboembolism, which can be evaluated separately with a lower extremity ultrasound.
